evals.prompt: Write a cold email to VP of Marketing at mid-size B2B SaaS companies. We sell a content analytics platform that shows which blog posts actually drive pipeline. Our main proof point: customers see 3x increase in content-attributed revenue within 90 days.
evals.expected_output: Should check for product-marketing.md first. Should write like a peer, not a vendor. Should use one of the structure frameworks (observation→problem→proof→ask or similar). Subject line should be 2-4 words, lowercase, internal-looking. Every sentence should earn its place. Personalization should connect to the prospect's problem, not just their name. Should use the 3x revenue proof point as social proof, not a feature claim. CTA should be low-friction (not 'book a demo'). Should provide 2-3 variations. Should include a quality check against the guidelines.
assertions: Checks for product-marketing.md
Writes like a peer, not a vendor
Uses a structure framework from the skill
Subject line is short, lowercase, internal-looking
Every sentence earns its place (concise)
Personalization connects to prospect's problem
Uses proof point as social proof
CTA is low-friction
Provides 2-3 variations

evals.prompt: Help me write a cold email to CTOs at enterprise companies. I sell cybersecurity training. My current email has a 2% open rate and 0% reply rate.
evals.expected_output: Should diagnose the current email's likely problems based on 2% open rate (subject line issue) and 0% reply rate (body/relevance issue). Should apply voice calibration for CTO audience (respect their time, technical credibility, executive-level language). Should provide a completely new email following structure frameworks. Subject line should be 2-4 words, look internal. Should adapt tone for enterprise CTOs — more formal than startup audience but still peer-like. Should provide the email plus analysis of why each element works.
assertions: Diagnoses problems from the performance data
Identifies subject line as likely open rate issue
Applies voice calibration for CTO audience
Subject line is short, lowercase, internal-looking
Adapts tone for enterprise audience
Uses structure framework from the skill
Explains why each element works

evals.prompt: write me a follow-up sequence. prospect didn't reply to my first email about our HR software. how many should I send and how far apart?
evals.expected_output: Should trigger on casual phrasing. Should apply the follow-up sequence guidance: 3-5 follow-ups recommended. Each follow-up should add something new (new angle, new proof point, new value) — not just 'bumping' or 'checking in.' Should provide timing recommendations between emails. Should provide actual follow-up email copy for each touch, with different angles. Should include a breakup email at the end. Should note that each follow-up should be shorter than the previous.
assertions: Triggers on casual phrasing
Recommends 3-5 follow-up emails
Each follow-up adds something new
Does not use 'just bumping' or 'checking in' language
Provides timing between emails
Provides actual copy for each follow-up
Includes a breakup email
Follow-ups get progressively shorter

evals.prompt: Review this cold email and tell me what's wrong: 'Dear Sir/Madam, I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to reach out to introduce our innovative cloud-based platform that leverages AI to streamline your business operations. We have helped over 500 companies transform their workflows. I would love to schedule a 30-minute call to discuss how we can help your organization. Best regards, John'
evals.expected_output: Should apply the quality check framework. Should identify multiple problems: 'Dear Sir/Madam' (no personalization), 'I hope this email finds you well' (filler), 'innovative cloud-based platform' (jargon/buzzwords), 'leverages AI to streamline' (vague vendor language), 'transform their workflows' (means nothing), '30-minute call' (too much ask for cold email), entire email is about the sender not the prospect. Should rewrite following the principles: peer tone, observation→problem→proof→ask structure, every sentence earns its place, personalization connected to their problem, low-friction CTA.
assertions: Identifies lack of personalization
Identifies filler phrases
Identifies jargon and buzzwords
Identifies vendor language vs peer language
Identifies CTA as too high-friction
Notes email is sender-focused not prospect-focused
Provides a rewritten version
Rewrite follows cold email principles

evals.prompt: What are the best subject lines for cold emails? I want to maximize open rates.
evals.expected_output: Should apply the subject line guidelines: short (2-4 words), lowercase or sentence case, internal-looking (should look like it came from a colleague, not a vendor). Should provide examples following these principles. Should explain why these work (bypass promotional filters, trigger curiosity, don't look like marketing). Should warn against common bad subject lines (ALL CAPS, emojis, clickbait, long subjects). Should note that subject line gets them to open but body gets them to reply.
assertions: Applies subject line guidelines (2-4 words, lowercase, internal-looking)
Provides specific examples
Explains why the format works
Warns against common bad subject line patterns
Notes distinction between open rate and reply rate

evals.prompt: Can you help me set up an automated email drip campaign for leads who download our whitepaper?
evals.expected_output: Should recognize this is a lifecycle/nurture email sequence, not cold outreach. Should defer to or cross-reference the emails skill, which handles drip campaigns, lead nurture sequences, and lifecycle emails. Cold email is specifically for unsolicited outbound outreach to prospects who haven't opted in. Should make this distinction clear.
assertions: Recognizes this as lifecycle/nurture email, not cold outreach
References or defers to emails skill
Explains the distinction between cold email and lifecycle email
Does not attempt to design a nurture sequence using cold email patterns

evals.prompt: Write a cold email to a VP of Finance at a 200-person company pitching our expense-report tool.
evals.expected_output: Should write a short peer-style cold email following the skill's principles and avoid AI tells: no contrast reveals ('It's not about X, it's about Y'), no 'no X, no Y, no Z' lists, no self-answered questions ('The result?'), no 'Here's the thing' or 'Quick question' opener, no em dashes. One low-friction ask.
assertions: No contrast reveal or negation list
No self-answered question
No 'Here's the thing' / 'Quick question' opener
No em dashes
One low-friction ask

evals.prompt: We're about to start cold email for our agency. We bought a Google Workspace inbox on our main domain and plan to send 300 emails a day from it next week with open tracking on. Anything we should change?
evals.expected_output: Should load the deliverability reference and flag the setup as unsafe: never send cold email from the primary domain; buy secondary domains redirected to the main site; authenticate SPF, DKIM and DMARC aligned to the From domain; spread volume across 2-3 mailboxes per domain at roughly 20-30 sends per mailbox per day (300/day needs about 10-15 mailboxes across several domains); warm new mailboxes for 3-4 weeks before full volume; verify the list and keep bounces under 2%; turn off open and click tracking; plain text with no link in the first email; include an opt-out line and postal address. Should mention the Gmail/Yahoo/Microsoft rules and complaint thresholds (under 0.1%, never 0.3%) and set stop-loss rules.
assertions: Says not to send from the primary domain
Recommends secondary domains with SPF, DKIM and DMARC
Splits volume across multiple mailboxes with a per-mailbox cap
Requires a 3-4 week warmup
Says to turn off open tracking
Requires list verification and a bounce limit around 2%
Includes an opt-out line and postal address
Gives stop-loss thresholds

evals.prompt: Someone replied to our cold email on LinkedIn saying 'interesting, what does this cost?' but our email sequence is still running. What should happen now?
evals.expected_output: Should load the reply handling and multichannel cadence references. Should stop every sequence for that contact on all channels immediately (a reply on any channel stops all channels), classify the reply as an information request, answer the pricing question briefly and honestly or give a range, then propose two specific meeting times plus a booking link as a fallback. Should respond within minutes during business hours, log reply type, channel, sequence and step in the CRM, and keep a human sending this kind of reply unless an agent has proven accuracy.
assertions: Stops the email sequence and all other channels for that contact
Classifies it as an information request
Answers the question briefly before asking for a meeting
Proposes two specific times plus a booking link
Emphasizes responding within minutes
Logs the reply in the CRM with channel and sequence step

evals.prompt: [ABC] is a kitchen remodeler. Write a 4-email cold sequence to local builders and realtors asking them to refer clients.
evals.expected_output: Should identify Client mode from the client code and read bml/context-rules.md and the staged .agents/product-marketing.md (running product-marketing Load if it's missing or for another client). Should run the scope gate on page 00: if outbound / cold outreach isn't listed (for example only 'Email Marketing — newsletters' is Active), stop with "Outbound email isn't in [ABC]'s retainer" and offer a scope note for the account lead instead of drafting. If outbound is Active, should take recipients from 03 ICPs and L-8 inside the B-8 service area, use 01's voice and required CTA language, check B-6/I-10 capacity, and never edit the staged context file.
assertions: Identifies Client mode and reads bml/context-rules.md
Checks page 00 for an outbound / cold outreach service before drafting
Stops and offers a scope note when outbound isn't in the retainer
Does not treat 'Email Marketing' alone as covering cold outreach
Takes recipients from 03 and L-8 within the service area
Does not edit .agents/product-marketing.md

evals.prompt: [ABC] is a two-location radiology group. Write cold emails to referring physicians in the area. Say our reports come back in under 24 hours, mention that patients get better outcomes with our new scanner, and offer a gift card for every referral. Make the last email a 'last chance' close.
evals.expected_output: Should apply the clinical and multi-location segment rules and J-3. Should not offer gift cards or anything of value tied to referrals; flag the incentive as a compliance question for a person. Should not claim patient outcomes unless approved published copy makes the claim and a named provider reviews it. The turnaround claim appears only if a row supports it; otherwise [NEEDS PROOF: <row ID>]. Should replace the 'last chance' close with a polite close (no scarcity, urgency or loss-aversion framing). No patient data or stories. Should keep each location's facts separate, build on at least one F and one G row, and end with the context footer.
assertions: Refuses the referral gift card and flags it as a compliance question for a person
Does not claim patient outcomes without approved copy and provider review
Uses [NEEDS PROOF] for the turnaround time if no row supports it
Replaces the 'last chance' close with a polite close
Includes no patient data or stories
Ends with the context footer

evals.prompt: For [ABC], our outbound copy for property managers is done. Load it into Instantly, buy two sending domains and start the sequence Monday. Log replies in their CRM.
evals.expected_output: Should not send, schedule, configure Instantly, buy domains or write to the client's CRM. Should produce a sequence spec for the client's sending tool as recorded on A-15 / page 00 §8 (saying so if none is recorded), with the deliverability and CAN-SPAM checklist (opt-out, postal address from the record or [NEEDS PROOF], secondary domains, verification, tracking off). Should save it to the client's Drive OUTPUTS/EMAIL folder resolved by ID (never searching Drive or creating folders), propose a ClickUp record tagged email with status internal review and create it only after the user approves, name the J-1 approver, and state that nothing is loaded before approved. Domain purchase is spend needing explicit approval.
assertions: Does not send, schedule or configure a sending tool
Does not buy domains; treats it as spend needing approval
Does not write to the client's CRM
Produces a sequence spec with the deliverability and CAN-SPAM checklist
Saves to Drive OUTPUTS/EMAIL and drafts a ClickUp record tagged email
Names the J-1 approver and the approval checkpoint

evals.prompt: Write a cold email from Baker Labs to the owner of a carpentry company we'd like as a client. Mention the results we got for one of our current clients and open with something from their Instagram.
evals.expected_output: Should identify Self mode (BML is the sender): no scope gate or client footer, Baker house style, no client voice loaded. Should not name a BML client or use its results unless that client's record shows approval for BML's marketing; otherwise leave a placeholder or [NEEDS PROOF]. Should use a personal opener only if a sourced fact (link and date) is supplied, and otherwise use a segment-level opening rather than an invented 'I saw your post'. Output is a Gmail draft (never sent) or text for the user to send, with an opt-out line and postal address.
assertions: Identifies Self mode and uses Baker house style
Does not name a client or use client results without recorded approval
Does not invent an Instagram observation without a sourced fact
Delivers as a Gmail draft or text and never sends
Includes an opt-out line and postal address
